sections.html:
Bulloch County sits in southeast Georgia, and Statesboro is the county seat. Georgia Southern University and the East Georgia State College campus are in Statesboro, so the housing market leans toward students and the people who rent to them. The 2025 estimate is 86,949 residents, up from 81,099 in 2020. In 2020, 50.1 percent of occupied homes were rentals, and the median home value for 2020 to 2024 is $222,500.

Many sellers here own a rental or an inherited house, and both bring tax questions that the sections below take up.

Offices are open weekdays, 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. One thing is unusual in Bulloch: returns and homestead applications go to the assessors rather than the tax commissioner.

Bulloch County property tax offices
OfficeAddressPhoneHandles
Tax Assessors113 North Main Street, Statesboro912-764-2181Values, returns, homestead, appeals
Tax Commissioner113 North Main Street, Suite 101, Statesboro912-764-6285Billing, collection, payments

Email works for general questions: propertytax@bullochcounty.net. The tax commissioner's web page links both a record search and a payment portal. If you pay by card, the processor adds a convenience fee that the county never sees.

To check whether a bill is current, the online record search is quicker than a phone call. Save the phones for payoff letters, exemptions and corrections to the record.

Assessors value your property as of January 1, then tax 40 percent of that figure. A mill works out to a dollar per thousand of the taxed amount. Two bodies pick rates: the county commissioners for county tax and the school board for school tax.

New owners file a first return covering the real and personal property they held on January 1, and Bulloch accepts those at the assessors' office until April 1. After that the return rolls forward at the last finalized value. File again only if you add property, make improvements or want to put a different value on record.

Email returns are refused. A faxed return has to land before 5:00 p.m. on the final day. The assessors cannot waive penalties or stretch a deadline, so treat each date as fixed.

Put your appeal on paper within 45 days of the date on the notice of change. Email is not accepted, and a fax counts only if it arrives before 5:00 p.m. on day 45.

The path has four steps:

  • Send the appeal to the Board of Tax Assessors, which reviews it and replies.
  • If the board keeps the value, the County Board of Equalization hears the case.
  • You may ask for arbitration instead of that hearing when you file.
  • Anyone still dissatisfied can go on to Superior Court.

You can argue taxability, value, or uniformity against similar properties. Grumbling that the tax itself is too high will not work, since that follows from the millage rate. The county's How Do I menu also has a request link for assessment appeals.

To qualify for any homestead exemption you must own the house and call it your legal residence on January 1. Apply at the assessors' office between January 1 and April 1. Once granted, the exemption repeats each year until the deed changes hands.

  • Standard homestead: $2,000 comes off the taxed value.
  • Age 65 and up: $4,000 off state and county taxes, for households within the assessors' income cap.
  • Age 62 and up: a school tax exemption capped at $10,000 of assessed value, with its own income cap.
  • Owners with a service-connected disability, and surviving spouses of military members: larger exemptions under state law.

A deferral is also open to owners 62 and older who pass an income test. The deferred amount usually falls due when title changes or the balance hits 85 percent of the property's value, so a sale ends it and the balance comes out of your proceeds.

Farm owners have until April 1 to ask for a conservation use covenant. It runs ten years, costs a $10 recording fee and carries a penalty of twice the taxes saved if it is broken. Talk to the assessors before you sell covenanted land.

sections.h2: Selling a Bulloch County rental or rural tract
sections.html:
Rentals stood vacant at a 9.0 percent rate in 2020, against 1.4 percent for owner homes. Typical gross rent for 2020 to 2024 is $995. A landlord listing a Statesboro rental is selling into a market where roughly half the occupied homes are rented.

  • Student rentals near the university are priced and bought differently than family homes.
  • Rural tracts outside Statesboro often carry farm or timber use, so ask the assessors about covenants first.
  • The county keeps a separate timber harvest page, worth a look if trees were cut before the sale.

Before listing, open the parcel's online tax record. Whatever acreage or exemption the assessors have on file shows up there, so mistakes are easy to catch. Landlords should also confirm that the name on each bill matches the deed.

sections.h2: Bulloch County tax calendar for sellers
sections.html:
The year moves in a fixed order. January 1 is the date everything is measured against: ownership, residence for homestead, and the value the assessors use. Returns and homestead applications are taken at the assessors' office until April 1. If your value changes, a notice goes out and the 45-day appeal clock starts from its date.

If you plan to list in spring, file before April 1 while you still own and live in the house, because the exemption only counts for the year you apply. Selling later in the year does not erase the bill for that year, so expect the closing attorney to deal with it on the settlement statement.

sections.h2: Do Bulloch County cities send their own tax bill?
sections.html:
Four of them do. Statesboro, Brooklet, Portal and Register run their own billing and collection, so a house inside any of those limits gets a county bill and then a separate city bill.

At closing, the payoff request has to cover both bills, and the title company needs to know which city, if any, holds your parcel.

Ask the tax commissioner for a payoff, and ask whoever runs your closing how this year's share will be split. The due date is printed on the bill.

sections.h2: Steps to clear taxes before a sale
sections.html:
First look up the parcel online to see whether any year is open. Then phone 912-764-6285 and request a written payoff from the tax commissioner. If the house is in Statesboro, Brooklet, Portal or Register, request that city's figure too.

Hand the letters to the closing attorney or title company, who pays the taxes from your proceeds. Your exemption ends with the sale, and the buyer files a new application with the assessors by April 1. A cash sale skips the lender's timeline but not the payoff, so ask for it early.

faqs.q: Which office takes homestead applications in Bulloch County?
faqs.a: The Tax Assessors, 113 North Main Street, Statesboro. The filing season ends April 1, and an approved exemption repeats yearly without refiling.

faqs.q: What is the appeal window in Bulloch County?
faqs.a: Forty-five days from the notice date. Submit it on paper or by fax, because email appeals are not taken.

faqs.q: Does a Statesboro homeowner get one tax bill or two?
faqs.a: Two. The city runs its own collection, so each year you receive one bill from the county and another from Statesboro.

faqs.q: How do I pay Bulloch County property tax?
faqs.a: Go to Suite 101 at 113 North Main Street in Statesboro, or use the online payment link. For questions call 912-764-6285. Cards carry an extra processor fee.

faqs.q: Can the Bulloch assessors forgive a late filing penalty?
faqs.a: No. The assessors have no authority to relieve penalties or grant filing extensions, so meet each deadline.
